idiom_name: type switch over interface values (switch v := x.(type)), coverage unchecked
implementation_notes: Go branches on the dynamic type of an interface value with a type switch, which is the idiomatic way to dispatch over a closed set of concrete types; the structure is hand-written and the compiler performs no coverage analysis, so a type switch without a default silently does nothing when a new type arrives. Keep the set sealable by convention - define an unexported marker method on the interface (isEvent()) and keep the concrete types in the same package - and give the interface a method whenever the operation belongs to the type instead of the switch. A linter such as the community exhaustive analyzer, or golangci-lint with exhaustive enabled, can approximate the check for switches over named integer types, but nothing in the toolchain proves coverage for interface type switches.
code_sketch:
type Event interface{ isEvent() }    // unexported method seals the set

func Handle(e Event) {
    switch v := e.(type) {           // dynamic type of the interface value
    case Click:
        move(v.X, v.Y)
    case Key:
        handleKey(v.Rune)
    default:
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("unhandled event %T", v))   // runtime, not compile time
    }
}
pitfalls: The compiler never proves coverage: an omitted case falls through to default (or does nothing when there is no default) and the failure surfaces at run time.
Sealing by an unexported interface method only closes the set inside the defining package; exported interfaces remain implementable elsewhere, so a type switch over them stays open.
Type switches cannot be used on type parameters, so generic code cannot dispatch per variant through a type-set constraint.
